one_liner: A narrow-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.6x fair value. Interesting below about $16.

profile.what: Chipotle Mexican Grill operates fast-casual restaurants serving burritos, bowls and tacos. It owns its restaurants instead of franchising them.
profile.money: All revenue is food and drink sold in its restaurants and through digital orders. Profit depends on sales per restaurant and the cost of food and labour.
profile.valued: Chipotle is valued on P/E at a premium to restaurants when traffic is growing. The multiple moves with comparable-restaurant sales and new openings.

summary.sentence: A high-margin restaurant chain whose earnings growth has paused.
strengths: Revenue has grown every year in the record.
Earnings cover interest many times over.
risks: Customers can switch at every meal.

meaning.what_it_does: Runs a chain of company-owned restaurants serving burritos and bowls made to order from fresh ingredients.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Restaurant sales; it owns its restaurants rather than franchising them.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: A simple menu and assembly line let each restaurant serve many customers at high margins.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Customers trade down as prices rise, or a food-safety incident damages the brand.

moat.summary: A strong brand and efficient kitchens, in an industry where customers can switch at every meal.

industry.summary: Restaurants change slowly, but customer traffic is sensitive to prices and the economy.

management.summary: Has grown without franchising or borrowing for buybacks; the chief executive changed in 2024.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow, capex held at depreciation: $1.6B a year: operating cash flow less depreciation and stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). Capex is running at 2.0x depreciation, so most of it is expansion, not upkeep. (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 7–13% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 15%; cost of capital 8.5%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
